text: The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God; God never ceases to draw man to himself, and only in God will he find the truth and happiness he never stops searching for.

section: Sacred Scripture — Christ the Unique Word
text: Through all the words of Sacred Scripture, God speaks only one single Word, his one Utterance in whom he expresses himself completely: Jesus Christ.

Faith seeks understanding because it is intrinsic to faith that a believer desires to know better the One in whom he has put his faith, while recognizing that God's mystery always remains greater than our grasp.

section: Providence and the Mystery of Evil
text: If God the Father almighty, the Creator of the ordered and good world, cares for all his creatures, why does evil exist? To this question, as pressing as it is unavoidable, no quick answer suffices; only the whole of Christian faith, centered in Christ's cross and resurrection, gives the answer.

section: God Brings Good Out of Evil
text: God is in no way, directly or indirectly, the cause of moral evil; he permits it because he respects the freedom of his creatures and, mysteriously, knows how to derive a greater good from it.
The cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ, and he calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him, associating them with his redeeming sacrifice so that human suffering is not wasted.

Being more closely united to Christ, those who dwell in heaven fix the whole Church more firmly in holiness; they do not cease to intercede with the Father for us, showing forth the merits they acquired on earth through Jesus Christ.

The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life; the other sacraments and all ecclesiastical ministries and works of the apostolate are bound up with the Eucharist and oriented toward it.

In the most blessed sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ—and therefore the whole Christ—is truly, really, and substantially contained.

Those who approach the sacrament of Penance obtain pardon from God's mercy for the offense committed against him, and are at the same time reconciled with the Church which they have wounded by their sins.

Interior repentance is a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return, a conversion to God with all our heart, an end of sin, a turning away from evil, with repugnance toward the evil actions we have committed and the desire to change.

Only God forgives sins; because he is the Son of God, Jesus says of himself that the Son of man has authority on earth to forgive sins, and by virtue of his divine authority he gives this power to men to exercise in his name.

section: The Beatitudes and Desire for Happiness
text: The Beatitudes respond to the natural desire for happiness that God has placed in the human heart in order to draw it to the One who alone can fulfill it.

Deep within his conscience man discovers a law which he has not laid upon himself but which he must obey; its voice, ever calling him to love and to do what is good and to avoid evil, is man's most secret core and sanctuary where he is alone with God.

Our justification comes from the grace of God; grace is favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us to respond to his call to become children of God, adoptive sons, partakers of the divine nature and of eternal life.
Great is the mystery of the faith; prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God, always flowing from humility before the living and true God.

section: God First Calls Us in Prayer
text: Whether we realize it or not, prayer is the encounter of God's thirst with ours; God thirsts that we may thirst for him.

The simple invocation of faith—Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner—combines the Christological hymn of Philippians with the cry of the publican and the blind beggars, opening the heart to both Christ's majesty and our poverty.

Contemplative prayer is a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus, an attentiveness to the Word of God, a silent love; it achieves union with the prayer of Christ insofar as it makes us participate in his mystery.

The habitual difficulty in prayer is distraction, and another is dryness; in dryness the heart is separated from God with no taste for thoughts, memories, and feelings, even spiritual ones—this is the moment of sheer faith clinging faithfully to Jesus in his agony and in his tomb.

At the announcement that she would give birth to the Son of the Most High without knowing man, by the power of the Holy Spirit, Mary responded with the obedience of faith: Be it done to me according to your word.
Mary is a virgin because her virginity is the sign of her faith unadulterated by any doubt and of her undivided gift of herself to God's will.

The fruits of charity are joy, peace, and mercy; charity demands beneficence and fraternal correction, is benevolence, fosters reciprocity and remains disinterested and generous, is friendship and communion.

The first commandment requires us to nourish and protect our faith with prudence and vigilance; by despair, man ceases to hope for his personal salvation from God, for help in attaining it or for the forgiveness of his sins—contrary to God's goodness and justice.
Human life is sacred because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God and it remains for ever in a special relationship with the Creator, who is its sole end.
